checks.claim: Key: the lines show neon's atoms give off energy only in set amounts (electrons at set levels; a drop gives a photon equal to the gap)
A white-hot filament (hot solid) gives a continuous spectrum; a thin glowing gas gives bright lines
Neon sign: low-pressure gas, electrons driven by high voltage excite neon atoms, which drop back and emit; nothing burns
Pure neon glows red-orange; its lines are mostly red and orange
Stem 'breaks instead into a few sharp bright lines' and context 'neon's few possible drops make its few lines'
checks.note: Neon is known for a RICH line spectrum, not a few lines: Wikipedia says its red-orange colour is 'due to many lines in this range' plus a strong green line, and the NIST handbook lists about 60 strong Ne I lines between 450 and 750 nm (a classroom spectroscope shows well over a dozen). A physicist would call 'few possible drops' wrong. Fix the stem to 'breaks instead into many sharp bright lines, mostly red and orange, the same every time' (or just 'into sharp bright lines'), and the context to 'neon's set drops make its set lines'.

checks.claim: Context: 'the strongest a red one at 640 nanometres'
checks.note: Grokipedia calls 640.23 nm the most intense visible line, but the NIST handbook gives 640.2 nm the same intensity (200) as 585.2 nm and 540.1 nm, and much higher intensities to the deep-red 692.9 nm (1000), 703.2, 717.4 and 724.5 nm (800). Safer: 'among them a bright red one at 640 nanometres'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: every colour held back by glass; light only while the gas burns; soaks up most colours and gives back the rest
checks.note: All wrong: glass passes all visible colours (the filament's full band shows it), there is no combustion in a discharge tube, and the lines are emission, not absorption or reflection.

checks.claim: Balmer lines all end on level 2; 3 to 2 is 656.28 nm red (H-alpha); 6 to 2 is 410.17 nm violet (H-delta)
Key: violet, as a bigger drop gives off more energy (E = hf; shorter wavelength = more energy)
Stem: the drop from level 6 is 'a far bigger drop' than from level 3
checks.note: 3 to 2 is about 1.89 eV, 6 to 2 about 3.02 eV: 1.6 times as big. 'Far bigger' is acceptable.

checks.claim: Context: 'Violet light carries about twice the energy of red in each photon, so hydrogen's drop from the sixth level gives violet light at 410 nanometres and its drop from the third gives red light at 656'
checks.note: 'About twice' holds only for the edges of the visible range (Grokipedia: 1.65 eV at 750 nm, 3.26 eV at 380 nm). Hydrogen's two photons here are 1.89 eV (656 nm) and 3.02 eV (410 nm), about 1.6 times; the 'so' makes a reader apply 'twice' to them. Fix: 'Violet light carries more energy in each photon than red, up to about twice as much, and hydrogen's violet photon at 410 nanometres carries about 1.6 times the energy of its red one at 656.'

checks.claim: Context: red comes from the smallest of these drops
checks.note: 3 to 2 is the smallest Balmer drop.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (red with more energy; violet or red with less energy)
checks.note: All wrong: the bigger drop releases more energy, and more energy means shorter wavelength (violet).

checks.claim: Flame colours: strontium crimson, copper green-blue, sodium bright yellow; lithium also crimson
Key: each element's electrons' energy levels are spaced in its own way, so its colours are its own
checks.note: Standard school explanation. Strictly, a Bunsen flame's strontium red and copper green come mostly from molecular bands (SrOH, SrCl, CuCl, CuOH) rather than single atomic lines (Grokipedia, Pyrotechnic colorant), so 'thin lines' in the stem could become 'thin lines and narrow bands' if the writer wants it exact; the key still holds (set energy levels of the element's own atoms and molecules). Not an error at grade level.

checks.claim: Sodium's two yellow lines at 589.0 and 589.6 nm
Flame temperature does not choose the colour
checks.note: Temperature can change brightness, never the lines' places.

checks.claim: Fireworks: strontium for red, copper for blue, sodium for yellow
Lithium and strontium both crimson; spectroscope tells them apart
checks.note: Lithium near 670 nm, strontium 640-660 nm.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: burns at its own temperature; strains colours out of the flame's light; atomic weight sets the colours
checks.note: None is defensible: emission is not set by burning temperature, is not filtering, and mass is not what sets the line places (isotope shifts are tiny).

checks.claim: Bunsen and Kirchhoff at Heidelberg, 1859, reading metals' flame lines through a prism
checks.note: Grokipedia: developed 'between 1859 and 1860 at the University of Heidelberg'.

checks.claim: Compounds: chloride, bromide, iodide, oxide, sulphate, carbonate
Flames of sulphur, alcohol, lighting (illuminating) gas, hydrogen and more, of very different temperatures
checks.note: Paper: sulphur, carbon disulphide/'carbon dioxide' (translation), aqueous alcohol, illuminating gas, carbon monoxide, hydrogen, detonating gas; 'the great difference between their temperatures'.

checks.claim: Key: the lines kept their places whatever the compound or flame
Quote: 'had no influence on the position of the spectral lines corresponding to the individual metals'
checks.note: Exact words of the English translation of the 1860 paper.

checks.claim: Sensitivity: less than a three-millionth of a milligram of a sodium salt
checks.note: 'less than 1/3 millionth mg. of the sodium salt'.

checks.claim: 1860 paper: method can be applied to the Sun and the bright stars
Wrong choices (lines moved with compound, flame, or both)
checks.note: All contradicted by the paper.

checks.claim: Fraunhofer, Bavarian optician / lens maker
checks.note: Born 1787 in Straubing, Electorate of Bavaria; made optical glass and objective lenses.

checks.claim: Hundreds of dark lines in sunlight, 1814
checks.note: About 574 lines, 1814.

checks.claim: Moon, Venus and Mars showed the Sun's lines; Sirius and Castor showed other lines
checks.note: Huggins and Miller 1864: 'Fraunhofer recognized the solar lines D, E, b, and F in the spectra of the Moon, Venus, and Mars'; 'Castor and Sirius exhibited other lines'. Wikipedia: Sirius and other first-magnitude stars differed from the Sun and each other.

checks.claim: Key: the star lines were made in the stars (same air, prism and lens as for the Moon and planets)
checks.note: Sound reasoning from what changed and what stayed the same; Wikipedia: Fraunhofer concluded the lines 'originate in the nature of the stars and sun'; MIT: he studied the spectra of stars and planets with a telescope objective.

checks.claim: Context: same lines with different glass ruled out flaws
checks.note: Roy 2025: 'The lines seemed to be invariant of the refracting object'; MIT: he used the lines as standards for comparing prisms of different glasses; Grokipedia: replication with multiple setups.

checks.claim: Context: two broad bands at the red end made by oxygen in Earth's air
checks.note: A (759.4 nm) and B (686.7 nm), telluric, molecular oxygen.

checks.claim: Context: never learned what made the lines; died 1826
checks.note: Died 7 June 1826; the explanation came from Kirchhoff and Bunsen in 1859.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: Earth's air, the prism, the lens
checks.note: All shared with the Moon and planets' light, which showed only the Sun's lines.

checks.claim: Comte, 1835: the stars' chemical make-up could never be studied by any means (paraphrase)
checks.note: AIP translation of the Cours de philosophie positive (1835): 'we shall never be able by any means to study their chemical composition or their mineralogical structure'. Fair paraphrase; not in quotation marks.

checks.claim: Sodium flame's two bright yellow lines sit exactly at the dark D lines
Kirchhoff, 1859: bright sunlight through a sodium flame made the dark D lines darker
checks.note: Bookseller's description of the French edition of Kirchhoff's solar-spectrum papers: in the autumn of 1859, when the solar spectrum was bright enough, 'the dark D lines were made much darker by the interposition of the sodium flame'; Roy 2025 (citing Weeks 1932): the dark line 'became even darker'.

checks.claim: Key: sodium gas soaks up the very colours it gives off
checks.note: Kirchhoff's law of absorption and emission.

checks.claim: Context: Kirchhoff concluded sodium is in the Sun's atmosphere
checks.note: '...dass in der Sonnenatmosphaere Natrium sich befindet' (1859).

checks.claim: Context: Comte died in 1857, two years before
checks.note: Died 5 September 1857.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: glare contrast; heat bending light; wave cancellation
checks.note: None is the accepted explanation; absorption is.

checks.claim: Janssen, India (Guntur), 18 August 1868, bright yellow line at the Sun's edge (chromosphere), at first taken for sodium
checks.note: 587.49 nm. (Some historians question how clearly Janssen singled out the yellow line, but Wikipedia, Grokipedia and the Science Museum all credit him with it.)

checks.claim: Lockyer in England, 20 October 1868; near sodium's D1 and D2 but on neither (D3)
Lockyer named it helium after the Greek for the Sun
checks.note: Wikipedia: Frankland's share in the naming is doubtful; 'helios', Sun.

checks.claim: Doubt, even mockery, for 27 years (1868 to 1895)
checks.note: 'much doubt (and even mockery)'; 'finally settled' in 1895.

checks.claim: Key: a gas from a uranium mineral glowed with that line (Ramsay, cleveite, 26 March 1895, acid treatment)
checks.note: Grokipedia: cleveite 'a uranium-rich mineral'.

checks.claim: Context: Lockyer and Crookes identified it; two Swedish chemists isolated it the same year and found its atomic weight
checks.note: Per Teodor Cleve and Abraham Langlet, Uppsala, 1895.

checks.claim: Context: coronium's green line (corona) was iron stripped of 13 electrons, shown in the 1930s, from the corona's heat
checks.note: 530.3 nm, Fe XIV (Fe13+), Grotrian and Edlen.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: seen in other stars; seen at later eclipses; measured more exactly
checks.note: None settled it; the 1895 gas on Earth did.

checks.claim: Hydrogen lines strongest in white (A) stars such as Sirius; weaker in blue-white (B, O) stars and in the Sun (G) and Betelgeuse (M)
checks.note: A stars: 'the strongest hydrogen Balmer absorption lines among all stellar classes'; Sirius A1V, about 9,900 K, prominent Balmer lines; Betelgeuse M1-2 Ia.

checks.claim: Payne, Harvard (Radcliffe), 1925, used Saha's ionization theory
Key: line strength mostly set by the temperature of the star's outer gas (ionization and excitation), not the amount of the element
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'differing amounts of ionization at different temperatures'; OpenStax: 'The primary reason that stellar spectra look different is because the stars have different temperatures'.

checks.claim: Context: hottest stars' hydrogen ionized; cooler stars' hydrogen in the lowest level; lines best near 10,000 K
Context: stars mostly hydrogen and helium; about 73 percent of the Sun's mass hydrogen
checks.note: 73.4 percent hydrogen, 25.0 percent helium by mass.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: amount of hydrogen; distance; speed toward or away
checks.note: Amount was the old reading Payne overturned; distance dims the whole spectrum; speed shifts lines, it does not set their strength.

checks.claim: Russell of Princeton, outside examiner of her thesis
checks.note: 'respected outside examiner of her dissertation'; director of the Princeton Observatory.

checks.claim: Quote: 'It is clearly impossible that hydrogen should be a million times more abundant than the metals.'
checks.note: Exact words, from his letter to her.

checks.claim: Quote: her figures 'almost certainly not real'
checks.note: Thesis: 'The enormous abundance derived for these elements in the stellar atmosphere is almost certainly not real'; Wikipedia: written to meet her reviewer's criticism.

checks.claim: Key: Russell held the Sun was made much as Earth is
checks.note: Physics World: 'a strong proponent of the idea that the Earth and the Sun had the same composition'; Wikipedia: her result 'contradicted the accepted wisdom at the time'.

checks.claim: Context: 1929, same answer by a different method; cited her: 'the most important previous determination ... is that by Miss Payne'
checks.note: Wikipedia quotes the 1929 paper 'On the Composition of the Sun's Atmosphere' with these words; Physics World: he cited her work.

checks.claim: Context: for years the discovery was credited chiefly to him
checks.note: 'generally credited for the conclusions Payne had reached four years prior'.

checks.claim: Context: Struve called hers the most brilliant thesis ever written in astronomy
checks.note: 'the most brilliant PhD thesis ever written in astronomy', about 40 years later.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: hydrogen too light to hold; burned away; faulty photographs
checks.note: None is documented as Russell's ground; his was the accepted Earth-like make-up.

unit_notes: One error, one uncertain, seven ok. (1) 9853be611c: neon does not give 'a few' lines; its red-orange glow is many lines (Wikipedia, NIST about 60 strong Ne I lines in the visible); say 'many sharp bright lines' / 'neon's set drops make its set lines'; and Grokipedia's 'strongest at 640 nm' is not borne out by the NIST handbook, where 640.2 ties 585.2 and 540.1 and the deep-red 692.9 and 703.2 nm are stronger, so say 'a bright red one at 640 nanometres'. (2) 0a6a8f92fb: 'about twice' fits only the ends of the visible range; hydrogen's 410 nm photon carries about 1.6 times the energy of its 656 nm one. (3) Optional precision in da41bd86c3: strontium's and copper's flame colours are mostly molecular bands (SrOH, SrCl, CuCl), so 'thin lines' could become 'thin lines and bands'; the key stands. Every quotation in the unit (Bunsen and Kirchhoff 1860, Russell's letter, Payne's thesis line, Russell 1929, Struve) was found in a source. Facts sheet F32's Russell 1929 quote is in Wikipedia's Payne article, not in Physics World.
